narrative_idea_gen: Narrated in clipped, affectless dispatches by Ruthann, the twenty-year veteran 911 operator of Furnace, Nevada, the story follows bright-eyed DEA agent Cole Sebring as he's planted undercover between the town's two warring fentanyl operations and proceeds to manipulate them against each other using tactics stolen scene-for-scene from every cop film ever made — his *Departed* phone-swap gambit, his *Point Break* trust-fall surfing trip with a cartel lieutenant, his *Donnie Brasco* "forget about it" catchphrase he won't stop using — each escalation more reckless and more plagiarized than the last, steadily hollowing out the naive kid Ruthann first heard stammer his badge number into her headset. The whole grotesque opera peaks when both factions converge for a shootout at the town's condemned water park, only to collectively lower their weapons and gawk in slack-jawed silence as Cole, now fully unmoored from reality and his own identity, BASE-jumps off the defunct waterslide tower reciting Al Pacino's *Heat* monologue into a bullhorn while fourteen actual FBI agents swarm the wrong address three blocks away. Ruthann logs each incident in the same four-word structure she uses for everything — time, location, nature of call, outcome — and it is precisely this flatness, this refusal to editorialize, that makes the slow, absurd destruction of Cole Sebring the most damning indictment of cowboy policing ever committed to a county database.

narrative_beats:
# Scene-Level Beat Sheet: "Furnace" (Working Title)

---

## Beat 1: First Contact — Badge Number Stammered Into Static

**Concrete Action:** Ruthann, twenty-year veteran 911 operator of Furnace, Nevada, receives a transmission from a voice she hasn't heard before — young, nervous, conspicuously out of place on her frequency. Cole Sebring stammers his badge number into her headset, identifies himself through whatever thin cover protocol the DEA has provided, and asks her to log him as a local contact. Ruthann logs the call the way she logs everything: time, location, nature of call, outcome. Four fields. No commentary. Through her dispatch we receive the town itself — Furnace, its two warring fentanyl operations, its condemned infrastructure, the slow desiccation of a place that exists primarily as a line item in someone else's jurisdiction.

**Narrative Technique — The Dispatch Voice as Radical Constraint:** Ruthann's narration is established here as a *form* before it is a voice. The four-field structure (time, location, nature, outcome) functions the way a sonnet's volta functions — it is a container that determines what can be said and, more importantly, what cannot. Every emotional response, every editorial impulse, every human reaction Ruthann might have to what she witnesses is compressed out of existence by professional protocol. The technique is *institutional flattening as narrative mode*: the story's prose replicates the epistemology of the dispatch log, in which a domestic murder and a noise complaint occupy identical syntactic space. This is the García Márquez deadpan translated into bureaucratic American English — not the narrator choosing not to editorialize, but the narrator's *job* forbidding it.

**What Makes It Memorable:** Cole's stammer. The beat must establish him as a human being *before* it establishes him as a type. That first transmission — badge number fumbled, voice cracking, the sound of a person who has rehearsed this moment using movies as his mirror — is the only moment in the story where Cole is entirely, uncomplicatedly himself. Every subsequent appearance will layer another borrowed persona over this original signal. The stammer is the baseline the reader will measure all his future bravado against, and it is Ruthann's recording of it — flat, procedural, unimpressed — that preserves it like a fly in amber.

**What Makes It Work:** The structural choice to begin with Ruthann *receiving* Cole rather than with Cole *arriving* is foundational. It establishes that this is not Cole's story; it is the story of Cole as *logged by a system that has no category for what he is about to become*. The dispatch format also quietly introduces the story's central formal tension: Ruthann's four-field structure is designed to contain and close incidents, but Cole will generate incidents that resist closure, that bleed between categories, that gradually make the logging system itself look absurd. The form is the first thing we meet. Its inadequacy is the last thing we'll understand.

---

## Beat 2: The *Departed* Phone-Swap Gambit

**Concrete Action:** Cole executes his first operation against the two fentanyl factions: a phone-swap con lifted beat-for-beat from Scorsese's *The Departed*. He clones a burner belonging to one faction's lieutenant, feeds doctored texts to the other side, and manufactures a paranoia spiral that results in a botched supply handoff, a minor firefight, and — critically — both sides believing Cole saved them from the other's treachery. Ruthann logs the firefight. Three calls in eleven minutes. She recognizes what Cole is doing not because she has seen *The Departed* but because she has dispatched responses to twenty years of men who have. She does not note the film reference. She notes the outcome: no fatalities, two injuries, one vehicle fire.

**Narrative Technique — Plagiarism as Characterization:** The first gambit introduces the story's satirical engine: Cole does not merely imitate movie tactics, he *is constituted by them*. His operational playbook is a filmography. The technique is *citational identity* — each move Cole makes is a quotation, and the reader's recognition of the source becomes part of the narrative experience. But García Márquez's neighbor-woman principle applies here in an adapted form: just as every character in "Wings" projects their own framework onto the angel, Cole projects Hollywood's framework onto reality. The difference is that reality, for a while, *cooperates*. The tactics work. This is more damning than if they failed, because it suggests that the world of small-town drug enforcement is already so saturated with cinematic logic that a borrowed script can navigate it successfully.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The gap between Ruthann's log and what the reader understands is happening. She records a vehicle fire. The reader sees a man performing a Scorsese set piece in a desert parking lot. That parallax — the same event existing simultaneously as bureaucratic data and as absurdist theater — is the beat's signature effect. The reader occupies two registers at once and will remain in that split for the rest of the story.

**What Makes It Work:** This beat must *succeed*. Cole's gambit has to work, and work well. The structural logic demands it because the story's arc is not about failure but about *the wrong kind of success*. Every victory here adds a layer of confirmation to Cole's delusion that movies are adequate preparation for reality. The phone-swap must produce real tactical results — disrupted supply chains, shifted allegiances, Cole's rising status in both camps — so that the reader understands: the tragedy is not that the playbook doesn't work. The tragedy is that it works long enough to destroy the person using it.

---

## Beat 3: The *Point Break* Trust-Fall and the *Donnie Brasco* Catchphrase

**Concrete Action:** Cole's operations escalate in both ambition and cinematic derivation. He takes a cartel lieutenant on a surfing trip — or Furnace's desert equivalent, some adrenaline-trust ritual lifted from Kathryn Bigelow's *Point Break* — and the absurdity of the transposition (there is no surf in inland Nevada; they are perhaps doing something with ATVs or cliff edges or the condemned water park's dry slides) does not prevent it from working. The lieutenant bonds with him. Simultaneously, Cole embeds himself with the rival faction using a "Donnie Brasco" persona, complete with a "forget about it" catchphrase he deploys with increasing frequency and decreasing awareness that he is doing it. Ruthann logs the calls generated by his operations. The calls are getting longer. The incidents are overlapping. Cole's voice on the frequency, once stammering, now has the clipped cadence of a man quoting dialogue he believes is his own.

**Narrative Technique — Serial Plagiarism as Escalating Self-Erasure:** The accumulation of film references is not a gag; it is a structural argument. Each new borrowed persona overlays the last without fully replacing it, so that Cole becomes a palimpsest of characters — Costigan from *The Departed*, Bodhi's mirror-companion from *Point Break*, Donnie Brasco's wiseguy — none of which are him. The technique is *identity as montage*: the reader watches a human being disappear behind a composite of performances, and the comedy of recognition (ha, that's from *Point Break*) curdles into horror as it becomes clear that Cole is no longer choosing these references. They are choosing him. The catchphrase — "forget about it" — is the key diagnostic. A catchphrase is language emptied of meaning through repetition, and Cole's compulsive use of it signals that his speech, like his identity, has become purely citational.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The desert-surfing transposition — taking an iconic cinematic moment and performing it in a landscape that makes it physically impossible or grotesque — is the beat's indelible image. It literalizes the story's theme: Cole is applying a borrowed template to a reality that does not fit it, and the result is simultaneously functional (the lieutenant trusts him) and deranged (they are doing trust-falls off condemned infrastructure in 110-degree heat). The image should be funny enough to make the reader laugh and wrong enough to make the laugh catch in their throat.

**What Makes It Work:** This is the story's accumulation beat, equivalent to the chicken-coop-as-carnival in García Márquez. The spectacle is growing. Both factions are now invested in Cole. Both believe he is theirs. The structural function is to build the reader's dread through *competence* — Cole is phenomenally good at this, in the way that a method actor can be phenomenally good at inhabiting a role while the person inside the role is disintegrating. Ruthann's logs grow denser here, the calls more frequent, and the four-field format begins to strain under the volume of incidents. This strain in the *form* is what signals the reader that the story is approaching a structural threshold. The container is being asked to hold more than it was designed for.

---

## Beat 4: The Institutional Void — FBI, DEA, and the Bureaucratic Sublime

**Concrete Action:** The story pulls back to reveal the institutional architecture surrounding Cole's operation. The DEA has a handler somewhere — perhaps in Las Vegas, perhaps in Washington — who is nominally supervising. The FBI has a parallel investigation into one or both factions that does not know Cole exists. Jurisdictional confusion, interdepartmental non-communication, and procedural lassitude create a void around Cole that is not malicious but systemic: no one is watching him because everyone assumes someone else is. Ruthann, the only person who has a complete log of Cole's calls, exists in a bureaucratic stratum so low that her data flows nowhere. She is a dead-end node in an information network. Her dispatch records are technically county property, technically accessible, and functionally invisible.

**Narrative Technique — Bureaucratic Negative Space:** Where García Márquez satirizes the Church through its absurd procedural responses (does the angel have a navel?), this beat satirizes law enforcement through its *non-response*. The technique is *institutional absence as structural presence*: the FBI and DEA do not need to appear as characters; they need to be felt as a void. Ruthann's logs — precise, timestamped, dutifully filed — become devastating precisely because they demonstrate that every piece of information needed to prevent the coming catastrophe *exists in the system* and is being processed by no one. The comedy is procedural: forms filed, databases updated, interagency memos unread. The indictment as well.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The detail that the FBI has fourteen agents who will eventually swarm the *wrong address* must be seeded here. It should arrive as a passing logistical fact — Ruthann noting an unfamiliar frequency, an uncoordinated operation in her jurisdiction that she logs and routes per protocol. The reader files it away. Its detonation will come later. The absurdity of the federal apparatus — massive, expensive, confident, and aimed three blocks off target — is the story's broadest satirical stroke, and it must be set up with the same affectless precision that characterizes every other entry in Ruthann's log.

**What Makes It Work:** This beat is the structural counterpart to Cole's escalating gambits. While Cole borrows from cinema to construct an identity, the institutions borrow from their own procedural mythologies — the interagency task force, the coordinated raid, the chain of command — and the result is equally fictive and equally dangerous. The parallel is the point: Cole is performing *cop movies*; the FBI is performing *being the FBI*. Neither performance makes contact with the ground truth that Ruthann's logs quietly, uselessly record. The beat also solves a practical problem: it explains why no one stops Cole. The answer is not conspiracy or malice but the banal dysfunction of systems designed to avoid accountability. The bureaucratic void is what makes the water park possible.

---

## Beat 5: The Hollowing — Cole Loses the Frequency

**Concrete Action:** A shift. Cole's calls to Ruthann's frequency change in character. The stammering kid is gone; so is the competent mimic. What comes through now is a voice that has lost track of which borrowed persona it is currently wearing. Cole drops a *Donnie Brasco* line in a context that requires his *Point Break* persona. He references scenes from films that have no tactical application — quoting *Scarface*, *Training Day*, *The French Connection* — as if his internal library has lost its indexing system and is now playing on shuffle. He calls Ruthann's frequency at 3 AM for reasons that are not operational. She logs these calls: time, location, nature (unclear), outcome (no action required). The "nature unclear" entries begin to accumulate. They are the story's seismograph, registering tremors in a personality that is coming apart.

**Narrative Technique — Formal Degradation Mirroring Psychological Degradation:** The four-field log structure, which has been straining since Beat 3, now begins to *fail*. "Nature of call" increasingly reads as "unclear," "unclassified," or is left blank. The technique is *form as diagnostic*: Ruthann's system was designed to categorize knowable emergencies (fire, assault, medical), and Cole's disintegration generates incidents that do not fit any existing category. The bureaucratic form, like the village's interpretive frameworks in García Márquez, cannot accommodate what it is encountering. But unlike the villagers, Ruthann does not invent a category. She leaves the field incomplete. That blank space is the most eloquent thing in the story.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The 3 AM calls. The reader needs to feel, through Ruthann's flattened prose, the specific loneliness of a person who has no self left and is reaching for the only human connection available — a dispatch operator bound by protocol not to respond as a human. Cole is calling Ruthann because she is the last person who heard him when he was still himself (Beat 1, the stammered badge number). He cannot say this. She cannot acknowledge it. The dispatch format forbids the conversation both of them
narrative_story:
# Furnace

---

## I.

The first time Cole Sebring contacted Nye County Emergency Dispatch, Channel 4, he could not get through his own badge number.

"This is — this is, uh. Sierra. Echo. Bravo. Zero-three — wait. Zero-three-seven. Niner. Negative, scratch that, zero-three-seven-nine. Suffix Delta-Echo-Alpha. Requesting — I'm requesting local contact protocol. Log me as — as a local contact. Please."

He said *please*. In twenty years of operating the Furnace, Nevada, emergency frequency, I have received calls from men who were on fire, men who had been shot, men who had shot someone and wanted to know if there was a non-emergency number they should have used instead, and one man who had driven his Pontiac Sunfire into an abandoned mercury mine and needed to be talked through reversing on a grade while the chassis scraped against timbers placed during the Coolidge administration. None of them said *please*.

I logged the call.

>**TIME:** 09:47:23 PST
>**LOCATION:** Furnace, NV — coordinates not provided, caller reported mobile
>**NATURE:** Administrative — federal contact registration, badge series DEA
>**OUTCOME:** Logged per protocol. No action required.

That is how the Nye County Dispatch Manual requires entries to be formatted. Four fields. They are adequate for nearly everything. A four-field entry can contain a house fire, a grand mal seizure, the death of an infant. It cannot contain commentary, and commentary is not something Nye County compensates me to provide. I am paid $22.40 per hour, before taxes, to sit in the dispatch room of a repurposed double-wide on Route 160, eighteen miles from the nearest structure that could be called a town, and to log calls. The dispatch room smells of mineral deposits and the vinyl adhesive that holds the ceiling tiles approximately to the ceiling. The air conditioning unit was condemned by county inspection in 2019 and replaced by a portable evaporative cooler that turns itself off at random intervals, which I have also logged, in a separate maintenance-request system that uses three fields instead of four. No one reads those either.

Furnace is not a town in any sense that would survive contact with a census worker inclined toward rigor. It was a town once — a mercury-mining concern in the 1910s, a borax waystation in the 1940s, a place where people who could not afford Pahrump settled in the 1970s. The mines closed. The borax operation relocated. What remains is a gas station that sells food, a food store that sells gas, a post office that operates on Tuesday and Thursday, and the Splashdown Fun Park, which was a water park for three seasons in 1994 through 1996 before the water table dropped below its pump specifications and the county condemned the slides for a reason the paperwork describes as "structural inadequacy compounded by thermal stress." The slides are still there. They curve over the desert like the ribs of something that died in a position of exertion.

Also remaining: two fentanyl distribution operations that between them service the eastern corridor from Pahrump to Tonopah. I know their dispatching signatures the way a birder knows calls. The Molina operation generates incidents primarily on weekends — loss-of-consciousness calls, domestics that correlate with pay cycles, vehicle accidents on the 160 involving drivers who, per the paramedics' notes, were "non-responsive to stimuli at time of contact." The Kreigel operation generates incidents primarily on weekdays, which suggests a more disciplined customer base or a different product cut or both. The two operations have coexisted for approximately four years through a territorial arrangement I have inferred entirely from dispatch patterns and could not testify to in any proceeding because inference is not one of my four fields.

Into this, at 09:47 on a Tuesday morning in March, came Cole Sebring's voice, cracking on the number nine.

I noted at the time — though I did not log, because there is no field for it — that he had the particular diction of a person who has practiced speaking into a radio by speaking into things that are not radios. There was too much air in his consonants. He said "niner" the way an actor in a movie says "niner," which is not the way anyone who uses a radio professionally says it. People who use radios professionally say "nine." The extra syllable is a Hollywood invention, or rather a military invention that Hollywood preserved past the point of its practical life, the way certain amber deposits preserve insects in postures of flight.

He was, I estimated, twenty-six. I was off by one year. He was twenty-five.

---

## II.

The first series of incident calls that I attribute to Cole Sebring's operations came six weeks later, on a Saturday night in April, and lasted eleven minutes.

>**TIME:** 22:14:07 PST
>**LOCATION:** Junction of Route 160 and Furnace Access Road, east lot of Crossroads Fuel & Dine
>**NATURE:** Report of gunfire, multiple callers (3), concurrent report of vehicle fire
>**OUTCOME:** Units dispatched. Two individuals transported to Nye Regional with non-life-threatening injuries (GSW, left forearm; GSW, right thigh). One vehicle (2004 Ford Econoline, white, plates unreadable due to fire damage) total loss. No fatalities. Incident report filed.

>**TIME:** 22:18:33 PST
>**LOCATION:** Same
>**NATURE:** Secondary report of altercation, physical, involving four to six individuals in east lot. Caller (identified as shift manager, Crossroads Fuel & Dine) reports participants "screaming about phones."
>**OUTCOME:** Responding units on scene. Altercation dispersed upon arrival. No additional injuries. No arrests. Incident appended to primary report.

>**TIME:** 22:25:41 PST
>**LOCATION:** Same
>**NATURE:** Caller (unidentified male) requests to file report that his "property was tampered with, a phone, someone cloned my shit." Caller became agitated when informed this was not an emergency dispatch matter. Caller disconnected.
>**OUTCOME:** Referred to non-emergency. No action required.

Three calls. The first was chaos, the second was aftermath, the third was the explanation, though it did not know it was an explanation and I did not log it as one.

What I understood, from the calls and from the radio traffic that followed, was this: someone had intercepted communications between the Molina and Kreigel operations and fed each side information calculated to make the other appear to be encroaching on agreed territory. The information was specific enough to be credible and false enough to produce exactly the level of confrontation that would be frightening without being fatal. Two gunshot wounds, both to extremities. One vehicle fire. The precision of the outcome was conspicuous. Chaos that lands in a controlled range is not chaos. It is choreography.

I had seen this before, or rather, I had dispatched the consequences of this before. Not this specific tactic — the phone cloning, the manufactured paranoia, the precise calibration of violence to produce maximum disruption with minimum mortality — but the *type*. Men in my jurisdiction have, over twenty years, attempted to play criminal factions against each other using methods drawn from a source library that is, if we are being honest about it, remarkably consistent. The library is cinematic. The methods are always somebody else's first. I have dispatched the aftermath of schemes borrowed from *New Jack City*. I have dispatched the aftermath of schemes borrowed from *Miami Vice*, both the series and the film, which produce different dispatch signatures because Michael Mann's sense of operational scale changed between 1986 and 2006. I once dispatched paramedics to a man who had attempted the "Say hello to my little friend" maneuver from *Scarface* with a weapon he was not strong enough to fire from the hip. That call required two fields of "outcome" notation, which the form does not accommodate, so I used the second line of "nature of call" and left "nature" to speak for itself.

The phone-swap tactic was from *The Departed*. I have not seen *The Departed*. I do not need to have seen *The Departed*. I have dispatched the results of *The Departed* four times since 2007, twice before Cole Sebring arrived in Furnace and twice after. The first two were amateur efforts — imprecise, escalatory, resulting in the kind of cascading violence that fills four pages of log entries and ends with a long paragraph in the Nye County coroner's weekly report. Cole's version was clean. Surgical, if you allow the word to apply to an operation conducted in a gas station parking lot by a twenty-five-year-old federal agent who, six weeks earlier, could not say the number nine without his voice breaking.

What I noted — and, again, did not log — was that in the aftermath traffic, both factions' communications contained references to a new associate who had warned them, who had tipped them off, who had, in the local phrase, "had their back." Both factions were referring to the same person. I knew this because both descriptions, relayed through panicked and fragmented radio chatter that I am not technically authorized to monitor but which bleeds into my frequency due to the equipment limitations of a dispatch operation running on a 2011 Motorola base station, matched the same vocal profile.

Cole Sebring had set a fire and then arrived at both doors offering a hose.

It worked.

>**TIME:** 22:25:41 PST — Addendum, personal reference note, non-logged
>
>This is not a field in the system. There is no field for this. I am writing it in the margin of my shift log in pencil: *This kid is going to get himself killed, and when it happens, it will generate between four and seven calls, and I will log each of them in the four-field format, and each of them will be adequate and none of them will be true.*

I erased it before end of shift. Pencil marks in the margin of official county documentation are a disciplinary infraction under Section 14.3 of the Nye County Dispatch Manual, subsection (b), "Addenda, Unauthorized."

---

## III.

Over the next three months — May through July — I logged forty-one calls that I attribute directly or indirectly to Cole Sebring's operations. I will not reproduce them all. The form becomes repetitive, which is the form's point, and the point's limitation.

What the forty-one calls describe, if read in sequence, which no one will ever do because they are stored in a filing system that organizes by date rather than by association and because the only person who has read them in sequence is me, is an escalation pattern I have come to think of as *scenic*. Each operation is larger, more elaborate, and more conspicuously derived from a specific cinematic source than the last. I use the word *scenic* because the operations have the quality of scenes — discrete units of action with rising tension, a climactic moment, and a resolution that sets up the next scene. This is not how criminal informant operations are supposed to work. This is how movies work.

In May, Cole took Ricky Molina's nephew — who served as a lieutenant in the Molina operation and whose name, per county records, is Ricardo Molina Jr., though everyone on the frequency called him Pequeno, which means "small" and which he was not — on what I can only describe, based on the dispatch calls it generated, as a recreational excursion involving the condemned slides of the Splashdown Fun Park.

>**TIME:** 15:32:18 PST
>**LOCATION:** Splashdown Fun Park (CONDEMNED — see County Order 2019-0447), Furnace, NV
>**NATURE:** Report of trespassing, two males observed on upper platform of Slide Complex C ("The Vortex"), condemned structure. Caller (Ruth-Ann Winstead, 3440 Furnace Access Road) reports individuals appear to be "climbing the thing" and "one of them is whooping."
>**OUTCOME:** Advisory issued. No units available (both Furnace-assigned units responding to medical call, Route 160 mile marker 14). Caller advised to re-contact if individuals appear in distress.

>**TIME:** 15:51:09 PST
>**LOCATION:** Same
>**NATURE:** Same caller. Reports individuals have descended the dry slide on what appears to be a "mattress or a cushion or something." Reports both individuals now on the ground, ambulatory, "laughing like idiots." Caller requests to know if she should still be concerned.
>**OUTCOME:** No action required. Caller advised to re-contact if situation changes.

Ruth-Ann Winstead, who called in the report, shares my first name but not my hyphen. We are not related. She lives in a manufactured home three hundred yards from Splashdown and she calls my frequency an average of four times per month to report activities at the park, which is condemned and unmonitored and therefore attracts the kind of activity that generates calls. I have logged her reports of teenagers drinking on the platforms, of coyotes denning in the wave pool basin, of a man she described as "naked from a distance but possibly wearing something flesh-colored, I'm not getting closer to find out." She is a reliable caller. When she said one of the men on the slide was whooping, I believed her.

What I understood was happening: Cole Sebring was performing the trust ritual. The specific cinematic source was *Point Break*, Kathryn Bigelow's 1991 film in which an undercover FBI agent bonds with his target through shared adrenaline — surfing, skydiving, the substitution of mortal risk for emotional intimacy. There is no surf in Furnace. There is no sky worth diving from. There is a condemned water park with dry fiberglass slides that curve forty feet over a concrete basin that has not held water since Bill Clinton's first term. Cole had looked at what he had and improvised.

They rode a mattress down The Vortex. In July. In Furnace. Where the average daytime temperature is 112 degrees and the fiberglass surface of a sun-exposed slide reaches temperatures that I once saw a paramedic describe, in his incident notes, as "consistent with a commercial griddle." They rode it, and they survived, and Pequeno — who had, up to that point, been the most cautious and least accessible member of the Molina operation, a man who did not let strangers within arm's reach — began appearing on the frequency in association with Cole. Trusted him. Rode a mattress down a condemned slide for him. Bonded with him the way Keanu Reeves bonded with Patrick Swayze: through shared proximity to a death that did not quite arrive.

It worked.

Concurrently — and the concurrence is what aged my dispatch logs from merely busy to structurally strained — Cole was embedding himself with the Kreigel operation using a different persona entirely.

>**TIME:** 21:07:44 PST
>**LOCATION:** Kreigel residence, 7780 Furnace Flat Road
>**NATURE:** Noise complaint. Caller (anonymous, routed through non-emergency, escalated to dispatch per volume of calls — four callers in twelve minutes) reports "party or gathering, very loud, sounds like an argument but maybe not, someone keeps yelling the same thing over and over."
>**OUTCOME:** Advisory issued. Responding unit reports gathering of approximately fifteen individuals in rear yard, no altercation in progress. One individual (male, mid-20s, unknown to responding officer) was speaking at high volume. Content of speech described by responding officer as "some kind of repeated phrase or catchphrase, like a bit, like he was doing a bit." Gathering dispersed voluntarily. No citations issued.

The phrase, which the responding officer did not transcribe and which I therefore cannot enter into the log but which I heard on the radio traffic because my 2011 Motorola base station has the frequency isolation of a paper cup, was "forget about it." He was saying "forget about it." He said it the way Al Pacino does not actually say it in *Donnie Brasco* — the real line, the real delivery, is quieter, more offhand, a throwaway that signified belonging — but the way people who are remembering the movie rather than rewatching it *think* Al Pacino says it. Loud. Emphatic. A performance of a performance of a performance.

He said it, by my count, eleven times in the portion of the gathering that was audible on bleed-through. He said it to greet people. He said it to dismiss concerns. He said it in response to a question about whether he wanted a beer.
